proposals.relationship: Credits Foner as her adviser and a central model for historical scholarship, teaching and public engagement.
proposals.evidence_note: Her own acknowledgment on p. xv calls Foner her adviser and her biggest debt, while also naming other Columbia teachers. Her 1999 article, p. 67, acknowledges support and constructive criticism. No single proprietary theory, sole authorship or independently inspected degree file is inferred. The acknowledgment was read in the 2014 reprint; the 2004 printing was not collated.

proposals.relationship: Uses Jacobson’s account of whiteness and credits his reading of the Impossible Subjects manuscript.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, explicitly attributes the formulation of a consanguine white race to Matthew Jacobson and identifies Whiteness of a Different Color (1998). The work identifies Matthew Frye Jacobson rather than a namesake. The reprinted acknowledgment, p. xvi, names him among readers of all or part of the penultimate draft. The conceptual and manuscript roles are consolidated here; his original book remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Credits Gerstle’s intellectual and editorial interventions with improving Impossible Subjects.
proposals.evidence_note: The acknowledgment, p. xvii, singles out Gerstle while also crediting series editors William Chafe, Linda Gordon and Julian Zelizer. The 1999 author note acknowledges his support and constructive criticism; the 2014 foreword, note 4, lists American Crucible among resources on racial history. Other editors' contributions are not assigned to him, and editorial assistance is not formal supervision. His original books remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Anderson’s imagined-community framework to historicize the nation and question nationalist assumptions in immigration history.
proposals.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 9, and the new 2014 foreword, p. xxi, explicitly invoke Anderson. The 1999 article, note 8, also cites Imagined Communities alongside Hobsbawm, Balakrishnan and Gilroy. This is a specific conceptual use, not agreement with all nationalism theory. Anderson's original book remains unread, and its editions are not conflated.

proposals.relationship: Uses Gilroy’s insistence on historically specific racisms in analyzing legal racial categories.
proposals.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 7, directly attributes the historical specificity of racism to Gilroy before developing the argument about classification in the 1920s. The 1999 article, note 8, also lists The Black Atlantic, but the preview lacks the original introduction's note 14, so the exact source of the quoted formula is not invented. Gilroy's original works remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Hobsbawm’s criticism of treating the nation-state as normative to frame immigration categories as historical constructions.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69 and note 8, explicitly names Hobsbawm and cites the 1992 edition of Nations and Nationalism since 1780, p. 192. Anderson, Balakrishnan and Gilroy are also credited in the discussion. This is a specific appropriation, not an inference from a shared topic. The cited edition is not asserted to be the first publication, and the original remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Uses Roediger’s whiteness studies among resources for relating immigrant ethnicity, class and racial formation.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, cites Barrett and Roediger's joint Inbetween Peoples and Roediger's Towards the Abolition of Whiteness. The 2014 foreword, p. xxiii and note 4, calls critical race and working class scholarship influential, listing The Wages of Whiteness and the joint essay among examples. James Barrett and other contributors retain credit. The later retrospective is not treated as the cause of the 2004 book; originals remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Treats Strangers in the Land as an important account of racial nativism from which to extend the study of immigration law.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, calls Higham's 1955 book the richest account, then identifies limits in treating the passage of restriction as the end of the story. This positive starting point coexists with her particular criticism. The reprinted acknowledgment, p. xvi, also includes Higham among scholarly helpers without assigning him an individual task. His original book remains unread.

proposals.relationship: Questions the limits of Higham’s nativism framework and its economic-downturn explanation of restriction.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 69, appreciates the classic account while arguing that legislative triumph narratives can obscure categories produced after enactment. The 2024 article treats eugenics as one cause and argues that nativist surges accompany structural change even during expansion, rather than simply cyclical downturns. Benton-Cohen retains credit for the Dillingham finding. This does not certify every historical example or refute Higham's entire work; the original books remain unread.

proposals.relationship: Invokes Brubaker’s account of settlement and naturalization to frame critically the American narrative of immigrant citizenship.
proposals.evidence_note: The introduction, p. 5, explicitly quotes Brubaker on citizenship as a normal sequel to admission for settlement, then develops a criticism of assimilation as an inevitable destination. The quotation serves as a conceptual frame. The original Brubaker text and the introduction's note 7 were not available in the preview, so no exact title or first edition is invented.

proposals.relationship: Cites Making a New Deal among studies relating immigrant assimilation to twentieth-century class formation.
proposals.evidence_note: The 1999 article, p. 70 and note 9, identifies Cohen's 1990 study as an example of the specified historiographical approach, alongside Gerstle and James Barrett. This is a bounded textual reference, not formal mentorship, an exclusive framework or agreement with the whole book. Cohen's original remains unread.
